before:
A central bank is an institution responsible for currency, monetary arrangements and banking-system functions such as acting as banker to government and banks. In Namibia the Bank of Namibia is the central bank. Its official [explanation of its functions](https://www.bon.com.na/About-Us/Our-Functions.aspx) describes responsibilities for monetary and financial stability, payment arrangements and services to government. These are system functions, rather than the ordinary task of opening household retail accounts. The distinction concerns what the institution does, not simply the size of its building or whether the word bank appears in its name.

Central banks commonly issue currency, maintain accounts for government and banks, manage reserves and support monetary and payment arrangements. Currency issuance does not mean the institution can remove resource scarcity by printing notes. Payments and credit still operate within a real economy with limited productive capacity. Support for a sound banking system benefits households and firms by helping exchange function reliably, but it is not a promise that every borrower will receive a loan or every investment will succeed. For a learner comparing institutions, ask whether the example concerns the monetary system and banking relationships or a retail service to a particular customer. A shop seeking an ordinary equipment loan would normally approach a commercial lender rather than assume a direct central-bank loan is available.

The Bank of Namibia’s main functions are: it issues Namibia dollar notes and coins; it is banker to the government, holding its accounts and advising it; it is banker to the commercial banks, holding their deposits and settling payments between them; it is lender of last resort, lending to a commercial bank that runs short of cash so that depositors do not lose confidence; it supervises and regulates banks so that they stay sound; it manages the country’s foreign-exchange reserves; and it carries out monetary policy. When household borrowing or inflation is rising too fast, it can raise the repo rate (the rate at which it lends to commercial banks). Commercial banks then raise their lending rates, borrowing becomes more expensive, and credit and spending slow down.

before:
A market is an arrangement bringing buyers and sellers into contact to exchange a product or resource. Buyers seek something they want and sellers offer it on terms they are willing to consider. Contact allows information about the product, quantity and payment to pass between them. The arrangement can exist without a sale being completed in every conversation: potential buyers may compare offers or decide not to buy. What matters is the connection through which exchange can be arranged.

A market is therefore broader than a building or a row of stalls. A vegetable stall is one familiar example, but a repair service booked remotely can also participate in a market. Markets can concern goods, services or resources such as labour. In each case identify what is being exchanged and who occupies each side. A person looking for paid work offers labour services, while an employer seeks those services. Saying that someone is a buyer in one transaction does not mean they cannot be a seller in another. The same household may buy groceries and supply labour.

A market’s role goes beyond bringing buyers and sellers together. The interaction of demand and supply in a market sets the price. Prices then act as signals: a rising price encourages producers to supply more and buyers to buy less, while a falling price does the reverse. In this way markets help decide what is produced, how and for whom, and allocate scarce resources (see topics 1.2 and 3.2).

before:
A seller of handmade bags could reach local passers-by at a stall and distant customers through electronic orders. Direct inspection may matter when customers want to check stitching. Distance ordering may matter when travelling to the stall is difficult. Neither channel is automatically cheaper or better: travel, operating hours, access, delivery and confidence affect the comparison. This links to exchange in topic 2.3 and introduces the buyer and seller decisions analysed in market forces in topic 3.2. First establish the market arrangement; then explain how the relevant information and constraints influence exchange. A market description should name the product and the people connected. A building with no arrangement for buyer-seller exchange is not established as a market merely because people gather there.

Buying and selling online is called e-commerce. Its advantages are that it is open 24 hours a day, reaches customers far away, lets buyers compare prices easily, and can lower the seller’s costs because no shop is needed. Its disadvantages are that buyers cannot inspect goods before paying, delivery takes time and costs money, internet access is unreliable in some areas, and there is a risk of fraud.

before:
For an initial-value calculation, find the percentage quantity change as the quantity difference divided by initial quantity, multiplied by 100. Do the same for price. Then divide percentage quantity change by percentage price change. To classify demand responsiveness, use the magnitude of that ratio. Keeping the percentage calculations visible helps identify an incorrect starting value or a reversed division. The final coefficient has no currency or physical unit.

At a bag seller, price rises from N$50 to N$54 while weekly quantity demanded falls from 250 to 220. Quantity change is minus 30; minus 30 divided by 250 times 100 gives minus 12 percent. Price change is N$4; 4 divided by 50 times 100 gives 8 percent. The signed ratio is minus 12 divided by 8, or minus 1.5; magnitude is 1.5, elastic. Revenue changes from N$12,500 to N$11,880, a fall of N$620. This supports the interpretation that the quantity loss outweighed the higher price in this example. Do not label the coefficient 1.5 percent. Write the formula and the percentage changes before the coefficient, so each step can be checked. Before calculating, write the initial and new values in pairs so price is not divided by quantity accidentally. After calculating, check whether the magnitude agrees with the percentage comparison: a 12 percent quantity response is larger than an 8 percent price response, so a result below one would signal an error. This independent sense check supports the arithmetic without replacing interpretation of the economic result.

before:
Use quantity supplied, rather than demanded, in a supply calculation. Suppose a basket producer increases weekly offers from 400 to 420 when price rises from N$30 to N$33. Quantity rises by 20, which is 20 divided by 400 times 100, or 5 percent. Price rises by N$3, which is 3 divided by 30 times 100, or 10 percent. Supply elasticity is 5 divided by 10, or 0.5. Supply is inelastic for this change: the quantity response is proportionately smaller than the price increase. The coefficient is neither N$0.50 nor 0.5 baskets.

The calculation describes the stated observations under the assumed unchanged conditions. It does not prove the producer is incapable of a larger response next year, or establish why this response occurred without additional evidence. Limited spare capacity could be a possible explanation if the case states it. A different calculation with a 30 percent quantity response to a 10 percent price change gives three, elastic; a 10 percent quantity response gives one, unit elastic. Compare the ratios rather than absolute unit changes. This links the worked supply calculation to the demand example: both divide percentage quantity change by percentage price change, but the quantity and economic interpretation belong to different sides of the market. Use consistent initial values and state the time period in the data. If percentages are already provided, no initial-value reconstruction is needed. For example, a supplied 6 percent quantity increase and 12 percent price increase give 0.5 directly. Retain enough figures during intermediate calculations to avoid changing a boundary classification through rounding. State the requested coefficient clearly, then use words to distinguish a smaller positive response from a zero response.

before:
Pricing and output policies concern the price a firm charges and the amount it chooses to offer. Market conditions affect its discretion. A firm facing many sellers of an identical product must consider buyers’ ability to obtain the same item elsewhere. In the perfect-competition model the individual firm takes the market price. A monopoly faces less direct rivalry within its defined market and can choose a price-output combination, but still faces demand and costs. A higher asking price is not proof that customers will buy the same quantity.

For consumers, competitive pressure can encourage lower costs, choice and attention to price or service. Monopoly power can weaken that pressure, allowing higher prices or less responsive service. However, a large sole supplier may spread costs over a large output or fund investment that smaller firms would find difficult. The consumer outcome depends on whether these potential savings or improvements are realised and passed on. Ownership size alone does not settle the judgement.

Pricing policies. Price competition means attracting buyers with a lower price, for example a price cut or a special offer. Non-price competition means attracting buyers without changing the price: advertising, branding, better quality, after-sales service, loyalty schemes, free delivery or convenient opening hours. A firm with market power may use price discrimination, charging different groups different prices for the same product. It charges a higher price to the group whose demand is price inelastic (for example business travellers who must travel on a set day) and a lower price to the group whose demand is price elastic (for example leisure travellers who can choose another day or seller). This can raise total revenue. It works only if the firm can keep the groups apart, so that buyers paying the lower price cannot resell to the others.

before: Suppose a sole supplier uses large equipment that reduces unit costs but proposes a higher price. The cost-saving possibility is a case for large-scale production; it does not itself justify charging more. Examine service quality, output, demand and how the savings are used. Equally, several small sellers may face high costs, so counting them does not prove prices must be low. Compare incentives and evidence under the stated conditions. This links to market forces in topic 3.2, demand responsiveness in 3.3 and economies of scale in 5.4. These are simple economic models for explaining choices, rather than a claim that a real business perfectly matches their assumptions.
after: A sole supplier’s large equipment may lower unit costs without justifying a higher price. Examine output, demand, quality and how savings are used. Several small sellers may face high costs, so their number does not prove prices must be low. Compare market forces (3.2), demand responsiveness (3.3) and economies of scale (5.4).

before:
Occupational choice is an individual’s selection of a type of work, subject to preferences, opportunities and requirements. Earnings matter because they support spending and saving, but work also occupies time, affects safety and can provide interest, skills or satisfaction. Wage factors concern monetary earnings; non-wage factors concern other job characteristics. A person comparing jobs therefore needs more than the headline monthly pay. Required qualifications, available vacancies and the ability to reach a workplace also affect which choices are feasible.

An applicant may choose a nearby N$5,200 job over a N$5,700 job requiring unpredictable night shifts. The extra N$500 is a wage advantage, while the working pattern and location are non-wage considerations. The choice is not irrational merely because it does not maximise stated earnings. Its quality depends on the person’s needs, alternatives and costs. Another applicant may reasonably prefer the higher-paying role. No single ranking follows from these figures alone.

Changing occupation differs from changing location. Occupational mobility of labour is the ease with which workers can move from one type of job to another. Geographical mobility of labour is the ease with which workers can move from one area to another. Labour is occupationally immobile when it lacks the skills, qualifications or training for other work, and geographically immobile when moving is limited by housing costs, family or cultural ties, or lack of information about jobs elsewhere. Training that lets a clerk become a technician supports occupational mobility. Moving towns while continuing as a clerk concerns geographical mobility. A person can experience both changes, but they remain separate dimensions. This links to earnings in topic 4.2 and employment in topic 7.2: a wage difference does not prove workers can immediately change jobs, since skills and movement can constrain access. When advising an individual, compare monetary rewards, relevant conditions and the practical requirements of each option before making a condition-based judgement. The individual’s priorities should be stated explicitly.

People can also choose self-employment (working for themselves) instead of being an employee. Self-employment offers independence, flexible hours and keeping all the profit, but brings irregular income, long hours, responsibility for any losses and no paid leave or employer pension.

before:
A gender earnings gap is a measured difference between male and female earnings for a specified population and comparison basis. The measure might concern hourly rates, monthly earnings or annual receipts. These are not interchangeable. A monthly average can reflect hours worked as well as pay per hour, and an annual average can reflect periods without paid work. State which population and measure the data describe before explaining the result. This avoids treating an undefined gap as though it were one universal statistic.

Possible influences include occupation mix, experience, paid hours, career interruptions, access to education or promotion, caring responsibilities and discrimination. Their relevance must be established from evidence. Gender itself does not determine an individual’s skill, work effort or productivity. It would be unsound to explain a pay gap by assuming one gender is naturally more productive or uniformly prefers a particular job. A raw average also cannot show that discrimination is either the whole explanation or absent. To investigate, compare like work and relevant circumstances while recognising that unequal access to opportunities may itself affect the observed job mix. An example comparing average monthly earnings of male and female groups can illustrate measurement. The example shows the difference between a measured gap and its causes.

before:
Firm size means the scale of operations measured by a stated indicator, such as output, employment, sales or capital employed. These indicators can rank firms differently. An equipment-intensive producer may employ fewer people than a labour-intensive service while using more capital. State the measure rather than calling one business bigger without a basis. The suitable size also depends on the market it can serve. A specialised local repair service may face limited demand even if the owner could purchase more equipment.

Finance and production requirements matter. Some activities require large indivisible equipment or a broad network, while others can be provided effectively on a small scale. Organisation can limit how fast expansion is managed. Owners may value control, flexibility or personal service and choose not to grow despite a possible financial opportunity. A small firm is therefore not necessarily unsuccessful or waiting to become large. A large firm is not necessarily more efficient on every task. Evaluate the relevant market, technology, available capital, organisational capacity and objective before recommending a scale. This links to integration routes, occupational choices in 4.1 and productivity in 5.2: combining activities changes the organisation, while the result depends on the resources and demand that support it.

A size recommendation should also acknowledge the indicator used. Output of unlike products cannot be compared by adding physical items without considering what they represent. Employee numbers may be useful for a workforce question, while capital employed may suit an equipment question. State the evidence and avoid implying that one indicator captures the entire organisation. The factors limiting growth may differ by business: a niche market can bind one firm while another has ample demand but insufficient organisational capacity. Explaining the particular limit makes the recommendation specific and reviewable.

Firms grow internally, by producing more and opening new branches, or externally, by a merger (two firms agree to join) or a takeover (one firm buys control of another). Integration is external growth. Motives for growth include higher profits, a larger market share, gaining economies of scale, spreading risk by diversifying, reducing competition, and securing supplies or sales outlets. Small firms survive because the market is small or specialised, customers want personal service, the owner lacks capital or wants to keep control, small firms can be flexible, and they supply parts or services to larger firms. Disadvantages of remaining small include higher average costs, difficulty obtaining finance and greater vulnerability to a fall in demand.

before:
Technical economies of scale are reductions in long-run average cost from production methods or equipment made economical by larger scale. Some equipment can perform a task efficiently but needs substantial output to justify its resources and operating requirements. A small operation may leave it idle, while a larger one can use it regularly. The mechanism is effective utilisation or a production advantage enabled by scale, not machinery being inexpensive merely because it is large.

At a bottle processor, a specialised filling line might handle large standard batches with less resource use per acceptable bottle than a small manual arrangement. Compare complete costs, suitable output and utilisation. A large line used for a few bottles or frequent unusual formats might lose the potential advantage. Additional capacity also does not prove that customers buy the output. Demand and distribution need to support use of the technique. A newer machine can improve a small firm through technological progress without the cause being greater scale; distinguish the changed method from the scale condition that makes a technique viable. This distinction protects the explanation from labelling any equipment purchase a technical economy. The question is whether larger operation allows a resource-saving technique to be used effectively and how that lowers average cost under the stated conditions.

before:
Communication diseconomies are increases in long-run average cost when greater scale makes information transfer slower, distorted or more costly. A message may pass through several management levels or between distant sites, creating opportunities for delay or misunderstanding. The resulting mistake can waste materials, require rework or leave resources waiting. The diseconomy is not the existence of a message or meeting; it is the scale-related resource cost relative to satisfactory output.

At a uniform producer, a changed size instruction may reach one factory late. Producing the wrong batch uses cloth and labour but does not meet the order, raising cost per satisfactory uniform. A larger firm could reduce this risk through clear responsibilities and a shared record, so size alone does not establish inevitable failure. Compare the process rather than stereotype the workforce. Communication improvements may themselves cost resources, and their value depends on avoided mistakes and delays. This also distinguishes the category from coordination: a message can be transmitted accurately while schedules still fail to fit together. Identify whether the initial problem concerns information reaching the right people or the arrangement of interdependent work. Both can occur, but the mechanism should not be counted twice without explaining their separate effects. A useful remedy must address the diagnosed information problem. Repeating more meetings may add time without making instructions clearer. A shared record can help if staff receive and understand the right version, while clear responsibility can prevent conflicting messages. Compare the resources used by the remedy with the avoidable mistakes it removes.

External diseconomies arise outside the firm as an industry grows or concentrates. Competition for scarce local land and skilled workers can raise rents and wages; congestion can delay deliveries and raise cost per unit.

Horizontal integration joins firms at the same stage of production in the same industry. Two bakeries combining their businesses provide a straightforward example: both turn ingredients into baked goods. They do not become vertically integrated merely because one is larger or uses a different building. The distinguishing test concerns their place in the production chain and industry, not their geography. A firm opening another outlet by itself is also different from joining an existing separate business, although both can enlarge operations.

Combining similar activities may allow shared facilities, larger purchases or removal of duplicated administration. It may also reduce rivalry between the former competitors. These are potential effects, not part of the definition. The firms may have incompatible systems, different quality routines or locations that limit practical sharing. A larger combined output must have sufficient demand to use its capacity. In a bakery merger, cheaper bulk flour might be offset by additional transport between sites. Evaluating the transaction therefore requires more than naming horizontal integration. First classify the relationship, then examine the possible mechanism and its costs. The question is what activities have been combined and how their resources or market position may change. A joining of similar firms may increase market share, but that possible effect is not the defining test. The classification still depends on stage and industry. If a case supplies no production relationship, ask what each business does before choosing a label rather than using its motive as a substitute.

Government acts as producer when public operations combine resources to provide goods or services. The output may serve access, safety or other social objectives that are not captured by sales receipts alone. Producing a service still means using productive inputs: staff, equipment, premises and management must be available and organised. A financial loss does not by itself show a socially valuable service should cease, but a social aim does not remove the need to examine cost and effectiveness.

Consider a public information centre serving a remote community. It provides assistance that residents might otherwise have difficulty obtaining. The benefit concerns the actual service and access, not the centre’s government label. If funding is limited, spending on the centre has an opportunity cost in other possible services. Evaluate whether the output meets the intended need and whether its resources are used well. Paying no fee at the counter does not make staff time or equipment abundant. It also does not prove the output is a public good: access and capacity characteristics must be considered separately.

Provision, funding and production can differ. Government may fund a service produced by an independent supplier, or produce it through its own operations. Read the case before assigning the producer role. A public purchase shows demand for an output, whereas direct public production means the government operation itself combines the relevant inputs. This distinction makes later policy analysis clearer by identifying which activity and responsibility the evidence actually describes.

Government produces goods and services for several reasons. Public goods, such as national defence, street lighting and police protection, would be under-provided by private firms because non-payers cannot be excluded. Merit goods, such as education and health care, are goods whose benefits to the person and to society are greater than people realise, so they would be under-consumed if left to the market; government provides them free or at a low price. Government may also run essential services, such as electricity, water, rail transport and postal services, through state-owned enterprises (parastatals). It does this to make sure the services reach every region, including areas a private firm would find unprofitable, to stop a private monopoly exploiting consumers, or to keep control of strategic industries.

Privatisation is the transfer of a state-owned enterprise, or one of its activities, to private ownership. Arguments for privatisation: the profit motive may improve efficiency, the sale raises revenue for government, competition may lower prices and improve quality, and taxpayers no longer cover losses. Arguments against: a private owner may cut unprofitable services to remote areas, a private monopoly may raise prices, workers may be made redundant, and government loses control of strategic services. Nationalisation is the reverse: the state takes an industry into public ownership. Government may subsidise a loss-making state enterprise so that it keeps an essential service or jobs, but the subsidy has an opportunity cost in other spending.

before:
Government acts as employer when it directly hires people for paid work in public operations. The employees provide labour services and receive remuneration under the relevant arrangements. Public work can involve many occupations, including administration, maintenance and specialised services. The ownership sector does not determine whether the job is manual, professional or clerical; those are separate occupational classifications.

Hiring staff can expand the ability to deliver a useful service when the right skills, equipment and organisation are available. If a public facility hires technicians but has no working equipment, employment numbers alone do not establish greater service output. Training, support and effective scheduling can affect how much satisfactory work is completed. Equally, an employee’s contribution cannot be judged from a government label without examining the task and resources. The economic comparison concerns the service benefit and the scarce resources needed.

A contractor’s staff and a public employee have different direct employers even when both work towards the same public project. This matters when describing the government as an employer rather than a purchaser. It also connects to earnings comparisons in 4.2: varied roles and conditions need a fair basis before comparing public and private rewards. Government employment can provide household income and support public output, while budget commitments and opportunity costs remain. A supported judgement identifies what work is needed and whether the arrangement delivers it effectively, rather than assuming either that public jobs are inherently unproductive or that more jobs necessarily mean a better service. A useful comparison also specifies the period. Hiring today can require induction before additional service is available, while an existing tool shortage may need attention sooner. Timing affects the feasible contribution of each option. Evidence should guide timing.

Government is one of the largest employers in the economy, employing teachers, nurses, police officers, soldiers, administrators and workers in state-owned enterprises. As an employer it provides public services, creates jobs in regions where private firms are few, and can reduce the number of people without work. The wages it pays become household income that is spent on goods and services, which raises demand, encourages firms to produce more and can contribute to economic growth. However, a large public wage bill must be financed by taxes or borrowing, and the money has an opportunity cost in other spending.

A direct tax is charged directly on the income, profit or wealth of the liable person or organisation. It identifies the relevant base and liability. It is different from describing the tax as progressive or proportional, which concerns how its rate relates to income or another base. A tax on personal income can have different rate structures; its direct classification alone does not specify the average proportion paid at every income.

A teaching levy of 10 percent on a stated income illustrates a direct charge on that income. The rate is hypothetical, not a current national rule. If a business pays tax on profit, the profit base must be defined before computing a payment; sales receipts are not automatically the same base. Use the tax base and rate supplied in the task. The statutory payer also does not by itself settle every economic effect. A business may adjust prices, investment or other choices when a tax changes, and those responses affect other people. Describe the initial liability and then explain any possible wider mechanism conditionally. This separates classification from the claim about who ultimately experiences the burden. For a clear explanation, the named base and the reason it is direct provide a clearer answer than merely calling it money paid to government. A numerical exercise should specify whether the base is income before or after stated adjustments. If no legal allowances are supplied, do not create them. The purpose is to apply the defined classroom arrangement, while keeping actual tax administration and current statutory rules outside the unsupported example.

An indirect tax is charged on spending or transactions in goods and services and is commonly collected through suppliers. It can raise the amount charged to a buyer or reduce the amount retained by a producer, depending on how prices and quantities respond. The supplier’s role in collection is distinct from the economic division of the burden. A case needs information about the actual tax and market before a precise effect can be calculated.

Suppose a classroom example adds N$2 per unit to a product transaction. If the seller passes it all into the price and quantity is unchanged, the buyer pays N$2 more per unit. Those are explicit assumptions, not a rule that sellers pass every indirect charge on fully. Buyers may reduce purchases and sellers may absorb some of the cost, with the result depending on alternatives and responses. Do not infer a household’s total tax burden from a single transaction without its wider spending and income information. Indirect describes the tax’s route and base, while regressive describes a declining income share as income rises. A tax on necessities can have distributional implications, but classification should be supported by the relevant pattern rather than assuming each indirect tax has one identical effect. The comparison should make the paid amount, price condition and quantity condition visible. A per-unit charge and an ad valorem charge also use different bases if an exercise introduces them. One applies an amount to each unit; the other a percentage to a stated transaction value. Use the definition supplied rather than treating all price-related tax calculations as interchangeable. No new legal rate is implied by either teaching form.

before:
An exchange rate expresses one currency’s value in another. Under market determination, a higher demand for a currency relative to its supply can raise its value, while a larger relative supply can lower it. Buyers of exports may need the exporter’s currency, and residents purchasing imports may supply domestic currency to obtain foreign money. Financial investment, interest incentives and expectations can also affect currency demand and supply. Reasons for fluctuations include changes in demand for exports and imports; tourism (foreign tourists must buy the currency); interest-rate differences that attract or repel investment funds; relative inflation (higher local inflation makes exports less competitive); speculation; and central-bank buying or selling of currency. Because the Namibia dollar is pegged one-to-one to the rand, it rises and falls with the rand against currencies such as the US dollar and the euro. An appreciation makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper; a depreciation tends to do the opposite (see 2.3). These mechanisms operate together, so one trade change alone does not prove the final rate movement.

For a market-determined currency, greater foreign demand for local products may increase currency demand if transactions require conversion. The resulting appreciation is conditional on the other influences, not a guaranteed response of every rate. A rise in relative interest returns may attract funds where risk and expectations support it, but investors make their own decisions. Namibia’s N$/rand parity is an institutional arrangement described in topic 2.3, so these market examples should not be read as a freely floating bilateral N$/rand forecast. A depreciation can raise domestic costs of unchanged foreign-priced imports. Whether it improves the current account depends on sufficiently responsive trade demand and whether supply can respond, as well as time and input costs. Keep the rate quote and response conditions visible. A quotation should be read before interpreting appreciation or depreciation. More domestic currency per foreign unit means the domestic unit is weaker against that foreign currency, not stronger because the printed number is larger. Foreign units per domestic unit use the opposite quotation direction. Topic 2.3 develops conversion; here the reason for a fluctuation must be kept separate from the arithmetic description of it.

To use output data for absolute advantage, first establish a common input basis. When the same resources can produce more of a good at A than B, A has the absolute advantage in that good. If resource amounts differ, greater output alone may simply reflect greater input. Alternatively, data about resources needed for the same output identify advantage through lower requirements. Read which form the question supplies before comparing numbers.

For the alternative maxima, A produces 30 cloth against B’s 12 using equal resources, an output difference of 18 cloth. It produces 15 grain against B’s 12, a difference of 3 grain. A therefore has absolute advantage in both. The difference has physical units; it is not a comparative-advantage coefficient. Do not infer that the alternatives can be produced together at those maxima. Each is what the resources could make if directed to that good. This common-resource assumption permits a fair output comparison and supports the opportunity-cost calculation in the next block. Without it, an explanation should state the missing basis rather than assign an advantage from raw totals. If the data instead give hours required per unit, the lower input requirement establishes absolute advantage. A larger number is then worse rather than better. This contrast shows why reading the table heading is part of the economic method, not a detail to skip before comparing figures. Output maxima and input requirements are different data forms.

Real income per head is price-adjusted income divided by the relevant population. It is also called real GDP per head (per capita): real GDP per head = real GDP ÷ population. Real GDP is nominal GDP adjusted for inflation, so real GDP per head shows the average quantity of goods and services available per person. The real adjustment removes the effect of price changes on the stated basis, while per head accounts for population size. These are separate steps. A higher real total can still give a lower per-person figure if population increases faster. Conversely, a country with a smaller total may have a larger average when its population is smaller. State the aggregate, price basis and population used.

A real income of N$120 million shared over 20,000 people gives N$6,000 per head. If the total becomes N$126 million with 21,000 people, the average remains N$6,000 despite the 5 percent total increase. This does not mean each person receives exactly N$6,000. It is an aggregate ratio, and different distributions can have the same mean. Income from unpaid or unrecorded activity and external costs may also be poorly represented by the chosen measure. Use the average as evidence about a dimension of resources, then examine distribution and other outcomes for a welfare judgement. The calculation is not a currency amount each household can claim or a guarantee that government provides the same sum. This links back to output in 7.3 and the comparison of indicators: a useful average has a precise scope and explicit limits. A per-head comparison also needs a consistent population boundary. An income total for one region divided by the population of another would have no clear meaning. Keep units compatible when totals are in millions, and label the average as money per person for the period rather than as a percentage.

The Human Development Index (HDI) combines health, education and income into a composite measure of human development. Its dimensions use life expectancy, years of schooling and income per head. Values lie between zero and one. A higher value indicates higher measured human development, but does not show every person’s living conditions or how income is distributed.

before:
Free trade permits international exchange without protectionist barriers, while protection uses measures to restrict imports or shield domestic producers. A tariff is a tax on imports. A quota is a quantity restriction rather than a tax, so it is a non-tariff measure. These instruments can affect prices, quantities, government receipts and who obtains access differently. Naming a barrier is not enough to explain its consequences; identify how it changes a decision.

Protection may give selected domestic firms time or opportunity to develop and can support some jobs where import competition is strong. Buyers may face higher prices or fewer choices, and domestic users of imported inputs may face higher costs. Other countries’ responses or reduced competitive pressure can create additional disadvantages. Benefits are not necessarily shared across all workers or firms. A claim for temporary support also needs a credible reason that the activity can become viable rather than remain dependent indefinitely. Free trade can support specialisation and choice, but adjustment costs can fall on particular groups. This links to comparative advantage in 7.4: potential aggregate gains do not imply painless or equal outcomes. Evaluate the stated objective, affected groups, duration and alternatives without assuming one instrument solves every problem. A tax and a quantity limit should remain distinct even if both aim to reduce imports.

Methods of protection include tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on the quantity imported), embargoes (bans on specified imports), subsidies to domestic producers, exchange controls and strict administrative standards. Reasons for protection include helping infant industries grow until they can compete, protecting domestic jobs (a tariff makes imports dearer, so buyers switch to local goods, raising demand for local labour), preventing dumping of goods below cost, raising government revenue from tariffs, reducing a trade deficit, and protecting strategic industries such as food or energy. Free trade gives consumers lower prices and wider choice, lets countries specialise according to comparative advantage, increases competition and efficiency, and opens export markets. Protection risks retaliation by other countries, higher prices and less efficient domestic firms.
